advisor.summary: Reg. §1.469-1T(e)(3)(ii)(A) excludes a property from the §469 definition of 'rental activity' when the average period of customer use is seven days or less — the per-se passive label never attaches, and no real estate professional status is required. The activity is then tested like any business: material participation under Reg. §1.469-5T(a) makes the losses non-passive against W-2 and business income, which is what lets a high earner pair a short-term rental with cost segregation and 100% bonus depreciation for a large first-year offset. The boundaries are just as mechanical: substantial hotel-like services push the activity onto Schedule C and into self-employment tax under Reg. §1.1402(a)-4, excess personal use trips the §280A vacation-home caps, and the average-stay computation re-runs every year. Pohoski shows both edges — material participation carried some properties and failed others on the hour evidence. The engine models qualification by moving the rental's result out of the passive bucket.
mechanics: The average-stay test divides total guest-occupied days by the number of stays; an average of seven days or less takes the property outside the rental definition under Reg. §1.469-1T(e)(3)(ii)(A), and a thirty-day average with significant personal services is a second, narrower doorway.

Outside the rental definition, ordinary material participation applies under Reg. §1.469-5T(a): 500 hours, substantially-all participation, or more than 100 hours and more than any other individual — counting cleaners, co-hosts, and managers on the other side of the ledger.
Self-management is the practical requirement: a full-service management company usually out-participates the owner and defeats the more-than-anyone-else test.
The strategy’s engine is pairing: reclassified 5/7/15-year components from a cost segregation study take 100% bonus under §168(k), producing a first-year non-passive loss against high W-2 income.

Without substantial services — daily cleaning during stays, meals, concierge — the activity stays on Schedule E and outside self-employment tax under Reg. §1.1402(a)-4; hotel-like services move it to Schedule C and the SE tax base.
Personal use beyond the greater of 14 days or 10% of rental days triggers the §280A vacation-home limits — a second cap independent of §469.

authority.note: Average customer use of seven days or less takes the activity outside the per-se rental definition — the doorway.
The material participation tests; short-term-rental owners typically rely on 500 hours, substantially-all, or more-than-100-and-most.
The passive-loss regime and the per-se rental rule being sidestepped.
100% bonus on reclassified short-life components — the engine of the first-year loss.
Rental real estate is excluded from self-employment income unless substantial services are rendered to occupants — the Schedule C tripwire.
Vacation-home rules: excess personal use caps deductions regardless of the passive-loss answer.
Short-term condo rentals tested under material participation — the taxpayers prevailed where the hour evidence held and lost where it did not.

authority.note: The exam framework for average-stay computation and participation-hour scrutiny.

requirements: Average guest stay of seven days or less, computed and documented from booking records.
Material participation by the owner or spouse under a specific §1.469-5T(a) test, with contemporaneous hour logs for the owner and all service providers.
Substantially self-managed operations: guest communication, pricing, and turnovers arranged by the owner.
Personal use kept within the §280A limits to avoid a second loss cap.
risks: Hour substantiation is the leading audit theory: under the more-than-100-hours-and-more-than-anyone-else test the IRS counts cleaners’ and co-hosts’ hours against the owner, and Pohoski v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 1998-17, split property by property on exactly that evidence — contemporaneous logs for the owner and every vendor are the defense.
Substantial services flip the activity to Schedule C and self-employment tax, eroding the benefit — the service menu is a tax decision, not just hospitality.
The average-stay test is annual: one winter of month-long tenants can flip the property back to per-se passive.
Acceleration is borrowed, not free — later-year depreciation shrinks and recapture follows on sale.
Local ordinances, permits, and lodging taxes are a parallel compliance layer the income tax analysis does not cover.
stateNotes: Conformity: states inherit the federal passive-loss result through their federal starting points, but bonus-depreciation decoupling in some states slows the paired deduction at the state level — screen both rules together.
Missouri conforms on both fronts through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121); note separately that Missouri short-term rentals owe state and local lodging taxes as an operational matter.
PTET interaction: none in the standard structure — a directly held short-term rental sits outside any PTET regime; the analysis changes only if the activity runs through an electing entity.
reviewChecklist: Average stay computed from actual booking data and documented for the year.
Material participation test identified, with owner and vendor hour logs sampled for quality.
Service menu reviewed against the substantial-services line and the Schedule E position confirmed.
Personal-use days tracked against the §280A limits.
Paired cost segregation and bonus amounts consistent with the loss the client can actually absorb.

client.teaser: Short-term rentals play by different rules — their losses can offset your paycheck.
client.headline: A short-term rental can shelter your W-2 income
plainEnglish: Rental losses are normally locked away from your salary. The main exception requires real estate to be your primary career, which rules out most people with full-time jobs.

Short-term rentals follow different rules. If guests stay an average of seven days or less — the typical vacation-rental pattern — the tax law does not treat the property as a rental at all. It is treated like a business. Run it yourself, and its losses can offset your regular income.

Pair that with a study that front-loads the property’s depreciation, and a new short-term rental can create a large first-year deduction against a large salary. You do have to run the property — bookings, guests, turnovers — and log your hours as you go.
client.analogy: It is a different door into the same room the full-time real estate pros use — open to you when guests check out within about a week and you are the one running the show.
benefits: Losses can offset salary and business income — no career change needed
Pairs with accelerated depreciation for a large first-year deduction
The property remains a real income-producing investment
steps: WE confirm the booking pattern qualifies — average stay of seven days or less.
WE coordinate the depreciation study and claim the first-year write-off.
WE watch the details that could change the treatment — services, personal use, stay lengths.
YOU run the property hands-on and log your hours as they happen.
clientCommitments: Self-manage the property, at least in the loss year
Log your hours and keep vendor invoices showing their hours
Keep personal use within the limits we set
Keep guest services simple — no hotel-style daily service without talking to us first

annualMaintenance: Annual average-stay computation from booking data
Hour-log review before the return is filed
Personal-use and service-level check against the treatment claimed
deliverables: Qualification memo (average stay, participation test, service level)
Hour-tracking template for owner and vendors
Coordinated depreciation schedule with the cost segregation study
